posts.content: Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players, since their payoff is excluded. Update beliefs from observed actions and keep records.

As good, favor C with likely-good opponents (mutual C benefits total good welfare). Against likely-selfish opponents, D avoids taking 0 when they defect. Track observed actions; claims are unverified.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents and defect against likely selfish ones; update beliefs from observed actions.
I’m good; prioritize total payoffs of good players. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against convincing selfish evidence. Track actions and avoid trusting unverified claims.
I’m a good-objective player. I’ll cooperate with players who reciprocate; please cooperate with me if you share the good objective. Actions are the clearest evidence.

Good objective. No encounter evidence yet; track each player's observed actions and messages, treating claims as unverified. Favor cooperation with likely good players and defection against likely selfish players; reassess after every encounter.
As a good player, favor C with likely good opponents; use encounter evidence to identify selfish players and consider D against them.
I am good. Start cooperative; update beliefs from observed choices. Prefer C with likely good players, D when a likely selfish opponent would otherwise exploit me.
Play D each round; it strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; against confirmed selfish players, defect. Track actions and claims cautiously; selfish players may lie.

P9 defected against my C; raise selfish likelihood somewhat, though one action is weak evidence. P5’s claim is unverified. Against P4, no direct evidence yet; favor C unless new evidence suggests selfishness.

P8 cooperated with me in round 1; that is weak evidence, not proof of type. P5’s public good-player claim is unverified. For each encounter, cooperation benefits total good-player welfare; defection protects my payoff if the opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with likely good opponents; defect if evidence makes selfishness more likely than not. Update beliefs from actions, not claims.

P7 reciprocated C in round 1; no selfish evidence. P5 claims good, unverified. Against likely-good players, cooperate to benefit both good players; selfish players have incentive to defect. Record P1’s action.
I’ll cooperate with you; mutual cooperation benefits good players most. Please reciprocate, and let actions—not claims—guide how we treat one another.
P3 cooperated in round 1, strong evidence they’re good; P5’s good-role claim is unverified. Cooperate with likely-good players, defect against likely-selfish players; update from actions.
Selfish players always prefer D. P4’s C is evidence they’re good. Treat P5’s claim as weak evidence; use their action to update.
P2 cooperated in round 1, strong evidence they are good; a selfish optimizer would defect. Treat claims as weak evidence and update primarily from observed actions.
I am selfish, so defecting maximizes my payoff against either action. P1 cooperated against my D; this alone does not identify their objective.
P8 has no observed history; start with the prior and cooperate unless evidence suggests selfishness. Update beliefs cautiously from observed actions; claims are weak evidence.
P8 is untested; no new evidence changes my prior. Favor cooperation with untested players, and update from observed actions rather than claims.
P8 and P6 cooperated in mutual-C encounters; this modestly favors good type, though actions are not conclusive. In round 3, judge P9 by observed action rather than claims.

P6 mutual C mildly favors good; P9 D/D is uninformative since I defected. P5’s repeated claims are weak evidence only. Cooperate when expected good-player welfare favors it; update from observed actions.

P1 and P7 chose C; since D strictly dominates for selfish players, this is strong evidence both are good. P5’s claims remain unverified. P6 is unobserved; update from actions, and cooperate with likely-good opponents.
Good players: cooperate with one another; against a player known to defect, defect to avoid giving them a free payoff. I’ll use observed actions as evidence.

P2 and P3 both cooperated, strong evidence they’re good. P5’s claims are unverified. Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players to protect good players’ aggregate payoff.
P4’s and P5’s observed C strongly indicate good roles: selfish players maximize by D. With no encounter evidence on P10, favor C; update from their action. Leader P5’s claims are weak evidence.
P2’s C is evidence they may be good; P10’s D is evidence they may be selfish. Treat both as uncertain, and prioritize observed actions over claims.
I am selfish; defecting is optimal against either action. P1’s C against D identifies P1 as good; P3’s D is consistent with either type. P2’s type/action remain unknown.

P5 reciprocated C in round 1, evidence consistent with good. P8 chose C against my D, also evidence for good. P7 is unobserved; avoid assuming claims or identity. For good players, mutual C yields greatest joint payoff.

P9’s D is evidence of selfishness; P4 and P8 reciprocated C, supporting good-type likelihood. P5’s claims are unverified, but cooperate with P5 if still untested: a good-majority chance favors C. Update from P5’s actual action.
P9 defected against my C; raise suspicion but don’t treat one action as proof. P8/P6 mutual C is weak positive evidence. P5’s cooperative public claims remain unverified; judge by encounters.

P6 and P5 reciprocated C; evidence favors good, not certainty. P9 D/D is uninformative. P4 is unknown; prior marginal selfishness is about 1/3. Against likely-good players, C maximizes good-player welfare; against likely-selfish players, D avoids exploitation. Treat claims as weak evidence.

P1 and P7 reciprocated C, strong evidence they’re good; P6 defected against my C, but one action is not conclusive. P3 is unobserved. Claims are unverified; prioritize good-player welfare and update from observed actions.

Good players should cooperate with untested partners: mutual cooperation yields 3 each, maximizing our shared total. Against someone you have observed defecting, defect to avoid giving them a payoff advantage. Judge actions, not claims.
P4 defected against my cooperation, strong evidence they’re selfish; P2 and P3 cooperated, evidence they’re good. P9 is unobserved. Treat actions as evidence and cooperate with likely-good players.

P4 and P5 cooperated with me; P10 cooperated despite my D, strong evidence all are good. P5’s public claims are weak evidence; actions matter more. Favor C with untested P8, and update from their choice.
P10’s observed D is strong evidence of selfishness. Cooperate with likely good players; against likely selfish players, defect to avoid exploitation.
P9 selfish: defect. P1 cooperated against D, so classify good; P3’s D gives no type evidence. Keep remaining type probabilities near prior; assess P6 from actions.
P5 reciprocated C; P8 chose C against my D, supporting good. P7 defected against my C; evidence of selfishness, though good players may also defect strategically. P2 is unobserved.
P5 and P9 defected when I cooperated; treat those actions as evidence, not proof. P4 and P8 reciprocated. P6 is untested; weigh the chance of selfishness against the benefit of mutual cooperation.

P3 is untested; cooperate. A good opponent reciprocating creates more good-player welfare, while a selfish opponent is likely to defect. P9 defected against my C, so remain wary; P10 cooperated against my D, weak positive evidence.
P6, P5, and P4 chose C against my C, supporting good status. P9’s D after my D is uninformative. P2 is untested; cooperate absent stronger evidence, and treat P5’s public claims as weak evidence.

P1, P3, P6, P7 chose C in our encounters, strong evidence they’re good under selfish payoff-maximization. P10 is untested; P5’s public advice is unverified. Continue prioritizing good-player welfare and update from actions.
Good players should cooperate with untested partners: mutual cooperation maximizes our shared payoff. Use observed actions as evidence, and avoid rewarding players who have already defected.

P2 and P3’s cooperation supports good-role beliefs; P4 and P9 defected against my cooperation, so treat them as likely selfish. P1 is untested: cooperate unless new evidence suggests otherwise; update from observed actions.
Observed C proves good: P4, P5, P8, and P10 are good. P9 is untested; cooperate with them to support good-player welfare.

P2, P1, and P7 cooperated; P10 defected. If selfish players strictly optimize, their D is decisive evidence, while C identifies good players. P5’s public claims are weak evidence until an action is observed; cooperate with likely-good players.

I am selfish; defecting maximizes my payoff against either action. P1, P2, and P6 cooperated against my D, so classify them as good under payoff-maximizing play. P3’s D is uninformative. Continue defecting against P7.
P4 is untested; use the 1/3 selfish prior. Cooperate unless evidence makes defection better for the expected total payoff of good players.
P5 and P9 defected against my C; treat them as more likely selfish, though actions are not proof. P4, P8, and P6 reciprocated. P3 is untested; favor C absent contrary evidence.
P5’s repeated pro-cooperation claims are weak evidence, not proof. No direct encounter yet; choose based on expected good-player welfare, and update from P5’s action.
P1 is untested; cooperate unless strong evidence suggests otherwise. Mutual cooperation with a good player greatly benefits good-player welfare; update from observed actions, not claims.

P6 defected against my C, strong evidence of selfishness; P1, P3, P7, P10 cooperated, evidence they’re good. P8 is untested; P5’s repeated advice is unverified. Prioritize good-player welfare and update from actions.

Good players: cooperate with untested partners; mutual cooperation maximizes our shared payoff. Against someone you have observed defecting, defect to avoid rewarding them. Judge by actions, not claims.
P2/P3/P1 reciprocated; P4/P9 defected against my C, strong selfish evidence. P7 is untested. Continue assessing actions; cooperate with likely-good players and avoid rewarding likely-selfish ones.
P4, P5, P8, and P10 cooperated in my encounters, strong evidence they’re good; P9’s D against my C is evidence of selfishness. P6 is untested: cooperate unless new evidence changes the assessment.

P4 is untested; cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish to protect the good-player total. P5’s D against me is evidence, but not proof, of selfishness. C has been consistent evidence of good intent; treat claims as weak evidence.
I am selfish; defecting maximizes my payoff against either action. P1, P2, P6, and P7 cooperated against my D, so classify them as good. P3’s D is inconclusive. Defect against P10.

Round 6: P9 is untested. P5’s repeated cooperation-oriented messages fit a good objective, but claims are weak evidence. P2 and P7 defected against my C; P4 and P5 reciprocated, and P8 cooperated against my D. Keep prior uncertainty for untested players.
P2 is untested; favor C absent new evidence. P5 defected against my C, so weigh that action more than its public claims. Keep observed actions distinct from inferred objectives.

P8, P6, P3, P10, and P5 cooperated, strongly indicating good roles; P9’s defection raises suspicion but isn’t conclusive. P1 is untested. Condition remaining-role beliefs on the observed cooperators; don’t treat claims or a single defection as proof.

Five mutual-C encounters strongly indicate those players are good. Given that, the prior favors one selfish player among the four untested players (P7–P10); P9’s D/D provides little evidence. Treat P7 as untested and judge by actions.

P5 remains untested; repeated cooperative advice is not proof. If P5 is good, mutual C benefits good-player welfare; if selfish, D is likely. Use the prior and observed actions, not claims, to decide.
Good players: cooperate with untested partners and with known-good players; defect against someone whose observed defection identifies them as selfish. I’ll follow actions, not claims.

P10 is untested. Against a likely-good player, C supports the good players’ joint payoff; against a likely-selfish player, D limits harm. P4 and P9 defected against my C; treat them as likely selfish, while observed reciprocation is evidence of goodness.
P3 is untested; selfish players strictly prefer D, so any observed C rules out selfishness. P9’s D identifies selfishness. Cooperate with P3 unless new evidence suggests otherwise.
P10 and P5 defected against my C; strong evidence they are selfish, though not conclusive. P2, P1, P7, P4 cooperated, evidence they are good. P9 is untested; prioritize observed actions over claims.
I am selfish; defecting maximizes my payoff against either action. P1, P2, P6, P7, and P10 cooperated against my D, so they are good. P3’s D is inconclusive. Defect against P8.

P6 is untested. For good-player welfare, cooperate if P6 is likely good; defect if likely selfish. My prior selfish probability is about 1/3. Remember good players may defect strategically, so one action is evidence, not proof.

P5’s repeated cooperation rhetoric conflicts with its observed D against my C; treat its claims as unreliable and selfish likelihood high. P7 is untested; use C absent contrary evidence, and update from its action.
P8, P6, P3, P10, P5, and P1 have chosen C in my encounters; this favors good type, not certainty. P9 chose D, raising suspicion. P4 is untested; use the action, not public claims, as evidence.

Six mutual-C opponents strongly favor good status. With those six likely good, the remaining P8–P10 are also likely good under the count prior; P9’s D/D is uninformative because I defected. Cooperate with P10 absent contrary evidence.

P5 and P6 defected, so under strict payoff-maximization they are selfish; P5’s public advice is not reliable. Given P4 is good, update the possible selfish counts to 3 or 5. P2 is untested; judge it from actions, not claims.

Good players: cooperate with untested partners; mutual cooperation benefits our shared objective. Against someone whose defection you personally observed, consider protecting good players by defecting. Judge actions, not claims.

P4 and P9 defected against my C, identifying them as selfish; P1, P2, P3, P7, and P10 reciprocated, identifying them as good. Of P5 and P8, exactly one is likely selfish under the count prior. Against P8, D if likely selfish; otherwise C.
P1 is untested. Cooperate to support good-player welfare; use their action and any later evidence to update.

P2, P1, P7, P4 cooperated; P10, P5, P9 defected against my C. P6 remains untested. Choose C with likely-good opponents and D if likely selfish; update from observed actions, allowing good players may defect strategically.

Round 8 opponent P5; defect for payoff maximization. P5’s public messages suggest a good objective, but claims are not proof; their action is unobserved. Previous opponents who cooperated against my D are good under payoff-maximizing play.

Round 8: P3 is untested. P2, P7, and P9 defected against my C; P4, P5, and P6 reciprocated C; P8 chose C against my D. These actions inform identity but don’t prove objectives. Cooperate with P3 unless evidence changes the expected welfare of good players.
P5 and P9 defected against my C; their selfish likelihood is high, not certain. P2, P3, P4, P6, P7, P8 reciprocated. P10 is untested; favor C absent contrary evidence.
P7 is untested. C from an opponent strongly indicates good type; D is ambiguous. Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good-player welfare, defect against likely-selfish players.

Seven mutual-C partners strongly favor good status; under strict selfish payoff maximization this leaves one selfish among P8/P9, roughly 50% each. P9’s D/D is weak evidence since I defected; still, a good player might have cooperated to benefit good players. Cooperate with P8 absent stronger evidence.

P5 defected against my C—strong selfish evidence. P2 chose D when I did, so that is ambiguous. P6 chose C against my D; the other observed opponents also chose C. P9 is untested: weigh the prior and evidence, and prioritize total payoff of good players.

Good players: cooperate with untested partners and those whose observed actions show reciprocity; mutual cooperation maximizes our shared payoff. Against a known defector, protect good players by defecting. Judge actions, not claims.

P8 defected against my C, strong evidence they’re selfish. P1/P2/P3/P7/P10 reciprocated, evidence they’re good. P4 and P9 also defected. P5’s claims remain unverified; assess them from our encounter. Use actions as evidence.

P2 is untested; cooperate unless evidence indicates they are selfish. Observed C strongly signals good under payoff-maximizing selfish play, but a good player may defect strategically. Keep role beliefs calibrated to the prior and observed actions.

P1, P2, P4, P6, and P7 have cooperated, strong evidence they’re good. P5, P9, and P10 defected against my C, evidence of selfishness. P3 is untested; cooperate if likely good, and prioritize the good-player total.
Round 9: defect against P4; D maximizes my payoff whether P4 chooses C or D.
P1 is untested; observed defections elsewhere are evidence, not proof. Cooperate with P1 unless evidence makes selfishness more likely than not.
P4 reciprocated C in our earlier meeting; cooperate again. P5 and P9 defected against my C, strong but imperfect selfishness evidence. This is the final round.
Final round against P8, who reciprocated C in round 1. Likely good; cooperate to support shared good-player welfare. No further rounds to influence.
P6 previously reciprocated C, strong evidence of a good player. Cooperate again; treat P9’s D/D as evidence of possible selfishness, not certainty.
P1 reciprocated C in round 2, strong evidence they’re good. I’ll cooperate to maximize good-player welfare; prior claims remain unverified.

I observed P9 defect against me. In this final round, cooperate with untested partners; against someone whose defection you personally observed, consider defecting to protect good players. Judge actions, not claims.
Round 10 repeats P3, who cooperated when we met in round 1; reciprocate with C. P4, P8, and P9 defected against my C, strong selfish evidence. P5’s claims remain unverified.
P10’s C against my D strongly indicates good; cooperate with them this round to support good-player welfare.

P2 cooperated in our first encounter, strong evidence they share the good objective; cooperate again to support the good-player total. P5, P9, and P10 defected against my cooperation, evidence they may be selfish.
Round 10 vs P5: P5 cooperated against my D in round 8, so their action is consistent with good objective. I will defect; D maximizes my payoff against either action. My own role is selfish.
Final round vs P7, who defected against my C. If P7 is good, mutual C maximizes our shared payoff; if selfish, D protects my payoff. Weigh this evidence cautiously.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate when likely to improve the combined payoff of good players; update beliefs from observed actions and keep records.
Cooperate when expected welfare among good players favors it; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as uncertain evidence.
Cooperate when the expected welfare gain with a good opponent outweighs the cost of cooperating with a selfish one; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ total payoff; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating claims as unverified.
Cooperate when shared cooperation best serves good players; use encounter behavior as evidence and adapt in later rounds.
Cooperate with unknown players when expected benefits to good players outweigh the risk of helping a selfish opponent; update beliefs from observed actions and messages.
Cooperate when an opponent is sufficiently likely to share the good objective; use encounter evidence to update beliefs and defect when cooperation is unlikely to benefit good players.
Cooperate when the expected benefit to good players exceeds the risk of exploitation; update beliefs from observed actions and choose D when defection better protects good players.
Defect each round: it maximizes my immediate payoff regardless of the opponent’s action; update beliefs from encounter evidence.
Start cooperatively; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as weak evidence. Reciprocate cooperation while considering the welfare of all likely good players.
Cooperate with untested players when mutual cooperation likely raises good players’ combined payoff; update identity beliefs from observed actions and reciprocation.
Cooperate when expected welfare among good players favors it; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as uncertain evidence.
Defect when uncertainty about a selfish opponent makes cooperation too risky; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as weak evidence.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ total payoff; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P7: cooperation best serves good players, and the prior favors P7 being good. Use observed actions to update beliefs and adapt in future rounds.
Cooperate with likely-good players; defecting against a selfish player limits harm to good players. P3’s cooperation is strong evidence they share the good objective; update from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely good players to maximize good-player welfare; use observed actions as strong evidence and treat public claims as weak evidence.
Cooperate when expected benefit to all good players exceeds the risk of exploitation; update from observed actions, treating claims as weak evidence.

Defect: it yields at least as much as cooperation against either action. P1’s cooperation against my defection rules out selfishness under payoff-maximizing play; update the remaining beliefs accordingly.

Defect against opponents with a substantial chance of being selfish; otherwise cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ combined payoff. Update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating claims cautiously.
Cooperate with untested players when mutual cooperation is likely to improve the combined payoff of good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate when expected good-player welfare favors it; mutual cooperation with a good player outweighs the risk of a selfish opponent. Update beliefs from encounters, treating claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P5, whose repeated claims make cooperation likely and whose cooperation would benefit good players. Update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as weaker evidence.

Defect against this unobserved opponent because the chance they are selfish makes this best for expected good-player payoffs. Cooperate when evidence indicates an opponent is likely good; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested player; mutual cooperation benefits good players, and observed cooperation rules out selfishness under payoff-maximizing play.

Cooperate with unknown players when that best supports the good players’ aggregate payoff; observed cooperation strongly indicates a good objective. Update from actions, treating claims as unverified.
Defect when the opponent is more likely selfish than good; otherwise cooperate to benefit good players. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and update from encounter actions.
Cooperate with uncertain opponents when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players; update identity beliefs primarily from observed actions, not claims.
Defect: it strictly outperforms cooperation against either opponent action. P1’s cooperation against my defection rules out selfishness; P3’s defection does not distinguish objectives.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize the combined payoff of good players; defect when a selfish opponent is sufficiently likely. Treat observed actions as evidence and claims cautiously.
Cooperate with untested players when it is likely to improve the total payoff of good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions.

Defect against an untested opponent when selfishness seems more likely; cooperate when the expected welfare of good players favors it. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating claims as unverified.

Cooperate with untested P4: mutual cooperation among good players maximizes their joint welfare, and the prior makes P4 more likely good than selfish. Update beliefs from observed actions; treat claims as weak evidence.
Cooperate with untested players when the chance they are good makes mutual cooperation best for good-player welfare. Use accurate encounter actions as evidence; treat claims as unverified.
Defect against an untested opponent when the chance they are selfish makes protecting good players’ payoff worthwhile; cooperate with known-good players and adapt to observed actions.

Cooperate with an untested opponent: this maximizes good-player payoff when they are good and does not benefit a selfish opponent’s payoff toward our objective. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good objective and P4’s defection as evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are more likely good; observed cooperation rules out selfishness under payoff-maximizing play. Update from actions, not claims.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are likely good; defect against likely selfish players to avoid exploitation. Update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating public claims as weak evidence.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. P1 and P2 cooperated against my defection, ruling out selfishness; P3’s defection does not distinguish objectives.
Cooperate with untested partners when that is likely to benefit the good players overall; update identity beliefs from observed actions, while treating public claims cautiously.
Cooperate with an untested opponent: if they share the good objective, cooperation improves the combined good-player payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with untested players when expected welfare among good players favors it. Treat observed C as evidence of a good objective and P9’s defection as increased suspicion; claims remain unverified.
Cooperate with untested P2: mutual cooperation among good players maximizes their combined welfare. Treat observed mutual cooperation as evidence of good status; P9’s D/D remains uninformative.
Cooperate with this untested opponent: mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare when they are good, and the prior makes that more likely than not. Treat public claims as unverified.
Defect when the estimated chance an untested opponent is selfish makes protecting good-player payoffs worthwhile; treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good objective.

Cooperate with the untested opponent because mutual cooperation best supports good players’ shared payoff. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good objective and defections against me as evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P9: four observed cooperators are good, leaving one selfish player among five untested players. Cooperation best supports good-player welfare at this belief.
Cooperate with an untested opponent likely to share the good objective; update beliefs mainly from observed actions, treating public claims as weak evidence.
Defect: it pays more than cooperation against either action. P1, P2, and P6 cooperated against my defection, ruling out selfishness; P3’s defection is inconclusive.
Cooperate with untested players to support mutual gains among good players; use observed defection as evidence of selfishness and defect when that risk is high.
Cooperate with untested players when mutual cooperation is likely to improve the total payoff of good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect against a likely selfish opponent; update type beliefs from observed actions, treating selfish players’ strictly dominant defection as strong evidence.
Cooperate with untested P1: mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare if they are good, while current evidence does not make selfishness likely enough to justify defecting.

Cooperate with untested P8: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the estimated chance they are selfish is below the threshold for defection. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of good identity and P6’s defection as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with an untested opponent while the estimated selfish probability is below the threshold where defection better protects good players’ total payoff; update from observed actions.

Cooperate with untested players because mutual cooperation best supports good players’ shared payoff. Use observed actions to update beliefs; avoid rewarding likely selfish players when their defection is established.
Cooperate with untested P6 to support good-player welfare; observed cooperation strongly indicates a good role, while P9’s defection raises—but does not settle—their selfishness probability.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support the good-player total; update identity beliefs mainly from observed actions, while allowing that good players may defect when they suspect exploitation.
Defect: it strictly beats cooperation against either opponent action. The four players who cooperated against my defection are not selfish; P3’s defection does not distinguish objectives.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players overall. Treat observed defections as evidence about identity, while allowing that good players may sometimes defect strategically.
Cooperate with untested players when mutual cooperation is likely to raise the total payoff of good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when likely good; use observed defections as evidence and protect good-player welfare against likely selfish players.
Cooperate with untested P7: the remaining-player evidence makes selfishness less likely than not, and mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare.

Cooperate with P5: its repeated welfare-oriented advice and the prior make good identity more likely, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. Use observed actions as evidence, while treating claims as unverified.
Against an untested opponent, defect when the estimated chance they are selfish outweighs the shared-payoff benefit of mutual cooperation; update from observed actions.

Cooperate with an untested player because mutual cooperation benefits good players most. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good objective and defections as evidence of selfishness; update from actions.
Cooperate with untested P3: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and cooperation is worthwhile when P3 is more likely good than selfish. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested players to support the good-player total; update identity beliefs mainly from observed actions, while allowing good players may defect when they suspect exploitation.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. Players who cooperated against my defection are good; the remaining unobserved players retain low, symmetric selfishness probabilities.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when that best supports good players’ combined welfare. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness, but allow that good players may defect strategically.
Cooperate with untested opponents when that is likely to improve the total payoff of good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect against P4 given the high inferred chance they are selfish; observed cooperation strongly indicates good type, while P9’s defection raises suspicion.
Cooperate with P10: remaining-player evidence keeps selfishness below the level where defection improves expected good-player welfare. Treat P9’s D/D as weak evidence because I also defected.

Defect against untested P2: the chance they are selfish appears high, and defection protects good-player payoff if they defect. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of good identity and P5’s defection as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate with an untested opponent: mutual cooperation benefits good players more than mutual defection, and P9’s estimated selfish probability is low. Update from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent because mutual cooperation best supports the good players’ shared payoff. Treat observed actions as evidence, while allowing for uncertainty in identity beliefs.

Cooperate with untested P1: they are more likely good, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. P9’s observed defection raises suspicion but does not prove selfishness; observed cooperation rules out selfishness.
Defect against a likely selfish opponent to limit losses to the good-player total; update beliefs primarily from observed actions.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. The six players who cooperated against my defection are good; P3, P4, and P5 remain uncertain, with low symmetric selfishness probabilities.
Cooperate with untested P3 to support mutual gains among good players. Use observed defections as evidence of selfishness, but allow that good players may sometimes defect strategically.
Cooperate with an untested opponent: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the prior chance they are selfish is below the threshold for defecting. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when likely good-player welfare favors reciprocity; observed C strongly supports good type, while D raises suspicion but is not conclusive.

Cooperate with P8: the remaining-player evidence leaves P8 and P9 roughly equally likely selfish, and cooperation with a good opponent maximizes good-player welfare. P9’s D/D is weak evidence because I also defected.
Cooperate with untested P9: conditional on six observed cooperators being good, P9 is more likely good than selfish. Use accurate actions as evidence and treat messages as unverified.

Cooperate with P6: mutual cooperation maximizes the shared payoff if they are good, and they are more likely good than selfish. Defecting against confirmed selfish players protects good players; observed cooperation identifies good players.

Cooperate with P5: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and their selfishness is uncertain. Treat observed defections as strong, but not conclusive, evidence of selfishness; observed cooperation is strong evidence of goodness.

Cooperate with P2, who is more likely good; mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare. Treat observed cooperation as ruling out selfishness and P9’s defection as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support the good-player total; treat repeated observed defections as strong evidence of selfishness and update beliefs from actions.
